messages.subject: How to handle known removals of unmarked animals
messages.subject_clean: How to handle known removals of unmarked animals
messages.body_plain: We are conducting a population estimate of wolves in Alaska using DNA-based capture-recapture methods. This past season was our 5th year and, as it turns out, the hunting/trapping season was shifted to earlier in the season and therefore coincided with our study period. Approximately 45 animals were removed by trapping or hunting from our study area during DNA sampling. Approximately 15 of them were ones that had been previously detected in our hair snares and harvest took place within 1 sampling occasion from the last detection. In those cases, it seems relatively straightforward to be able to mark those identified animals as a known removal (i.e., treat them as being removed at the last sampling occasion). However, that leaves around 30 animals that were known to have been removed but had not been previously identified. To complicate matters, hunter/trapper reporting of harvest location is not very precise, with location usually reported only to the scale of watershed, peninsula, or other large geographical feature. Timing of those harvests are only known to within a 2-week period. These removals potentially represent a very large proportion of the total number of animals in the study area (up to 30% of the previous year's population estimate). Is there something I can do to include these unmarked removals in the analysis?

messages.subject_clean: How to handle known removals of unmarked animals
messages.body_plain:
I think there's no snap answer. Properly, you need to allow for both the spatial and temporal distribution of removals, as you understand. This could in theory be done by interleaving sampling 'occasions' with two detector arrays of differing type (hair snare and hunting/removal), and coding all detections on the hunting array as removals. I know you have only approximate locations for removals, but they may still be better than nothing. The two detector arrays form one traps object with a vector-valued detector type. I would use the 'multi' detector type across a coarse grid across hunted areas for the removal phases, and also specify binary usage for each 'detector' to distinguish snare and hunting occasions. I cannot be 100% sure that 'secr' will handle this without trying it.
Murray

messages.body_plain:
Hello Barkatullah

I think it is poor practice to perform an elaborate analysis of such meagre data. However, I appreciate this is an opportunity for you to learn about the methods, so I'll restrain my scepticism. I won't answer your question about time varying covariates - that is a fancy twist that is often unnecessary even for much larger datasets.

There are several ways to constrain a mask and include covariates. Here is one; replace names as appropriate. You will need the rgdal package.
datadir <- [your folder with shapefile]
# read polygon shapefile as SpatialPolygonsDataFrame object
SPDF <- rgdal::readOGR(dsn = paste0(datadir, "/habitat.shp"))
tr <- traps(snowleopardCH)
msk <- make.mask(tr, buffer = 10000)  # or whatever buffer you choose
msk <- addCovariates(msk, SPDF)       # look up mask covariates in SPDF
msk <- subset(msk, covariates(msk)$Habitat == 1)  # retain only those mask points with Habitat = 1

plot(msk)
plot(tr, add = TRUE)

It seems that a discrepancy between E.N and R.N arises in 'secr' with models that include individual variation in detection (both my earlier examples fit2 and fit3 are of this type). The code only considered the detection probability (and effective sampling area esa) of the first animal. The problem has been there forever. The sensible path is to take the harmonic mean of the individual esa as is done when computing H-T estimates of density in derived(). I have made this 1-line change to the internal function sumDpdot that is called by region.N() and re-built the package. This passes routine checks but won't be on CRAN until later in September (I'm traveling and CRAN incoming has a long maintenance shut down in early Sept.). Meantime you can access it at https://www.otago.ac.nz/density/zip/secr_3.1.7.zip (Windows binary) or https://www.otago.ac.nz/density/zip/secr_3.1.7.tar.gz (source). <https://www.otago.ac.nz/density/zip/secr_3.1.7.tar.gz>

Hi Roberto

Your results don't look so bad to me. Density is always animals per hectare - multiply by 100 for animals / km^2 (0.5 foxes/km^2?). The interim values shown during likelihood maximisation (trace = TRUE) are on the link scale (i.e. log of D, log of sigma).

I think you need a much larger buffer (>=6000 not 700 m, given sigma 1500-2000 m). Maybe also you can clip parts of the mask as 'non-habitat'. And at present you don't actually use zonemask; replace buffer = 700 with mask = zonemask in your call to secr.fit.

I note that secr.fit is painfully slow with your data (my test has barely begun) - I guess that's because you searched several fairly complex polygons. It is appropriate to use the 'polygon' detector type because foxes may be detected in more than one polygon per occasion, but for experimentation you might find it expedient (faster) to use the polygonX detector type.

Murray

Hi Greg
I attach an old pdf that may gives some clues to my prejudice against groups (less stable code, as sometimes revealed on this list).

Remember the hcov approach estimates combined density of both sexes together, and the default with groups = 'sex' (D~1) is to assume 50:50 group (sex) mixture.

The AIC code includes this line:
    AICcval <- ifelse ((n - Npar - 1)>0,
                       2*(secr$fit$value + Npar) + 2 * Npar * (Npar+1) / (n - Npar - 1),
                       NA)

Maybe you have a lot of parameters (Npar) and not many animals (n)?
Murray
